newsitem.title: CANADA: Battered Canadian dollar hits 2-year low.
newsitem.headline: Battered Canadian dollar hits 2-year low.

text.p: The Canadian dollar was under siege on Friday, pounded to a two-year low by signs of rising U.S. inflation and signals that Canada's central bank may resist hiking domestic interest rates.
The currency was trading at C$1.3982 (71.52 U.S. cents) -- its lowest point since April 3, 1995 -- as investors unloaded the dollar in heavy selling.
Bank of Canada intervention to buy the dollar and support it at the C$1.3960 (71.63 U.S. cents) level on Friday failed to stem the markets' strong anti-Canada bias.
"The dollar is vulnerable right now. It could easily hit C$1.4000 (71.42 U.S. cents) before it rebounds," said John Anania, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada.
Friday's sell-off followed U.S. indicators showing inflation worries were reviving in the United States.
The U.S. Commerce Department reported that the core producer price index rose by a higher than expected 0.4 percent in March, with retail sales growing 0.2 percent.

Analysts said U.S. inflationary pressures could push the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates again in May and force the Bank of Canada to raise its rates in defense of the flagging Canadian dollar.

A 25-basis-point rate hike by the Fed on March 25 widened the spread between U.S. and Canadian short-term rates to more than 200 points, pressuring the Canadian dollar and renewing calls for the Bank of Canada to follow suit.
Canada's dollar has shed almost four percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since January as investors moved to buy the higher yielding U.S. short-term securities.
"Canada (the dollar) is going to get hurt in this environment of rising U.S. interest rates," said William Chin, vice-president of foreign exchange with ABN-AMRO Bank.
He added that the central bank was unlikely to raise interest rates, now at 30-year lows after 11 interest rate cuts last year.

Early last year, the Bank of Canada began pursuing a "made in Canada" interest rate policy aimed at revitalising Canada's lackluster economy. The bank's rate slashing last year was independent of action by the Fed.

Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Timothy Noel may have tipped the central bank's hand on Thursday when he told Reuters in Lima, Peru that the central bank would not react to "every wiggle" in the currency.
"The bank does not want to react to every wiggle in the dollar," said Noel, adding that the bank would raise interest rates only if monetary conditions warranted such a move.
Noel's comments triggered a slide in the Canada dollar on Thursday, forcing the bank to intervene and to shore up the currency.

But Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Charles Freedman appeared to step back from those remarks on Friday when he said at a conference in New York that the central bank kept close tabs on exchange rate movements.
But some economists said the beating of the drums for a Canadian interest rate hike flew in the face of Canada's economic situation.

"The Bank of Canada is focused on deflation. A cheaper Canadian dollar helps them with that battle by easing overall monetary conditions and by pushing domestic prices up," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist with High Frequency Economics, in a commentary released on Friday.
The persistent challenging of the central bank to do something about the falling dollar "is getting boring," Weinberg said.
